claim: Ageing is associated with increased vulnerability to environmental cold exposure.
source: Ageing is associated with increased vulnerability to environmental cold exposure.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact that motivates the study.

claim: TRPA1 and TRPM8 receptors function as vascular cold sensors in mouse skin.
source: Previously, we identified the role of the cold-sensitive transient receptor potential (TRP) A1, M8 receptors as vascular cold sensors in mouse skin.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Behavioural responses to skin local environmental cooling are impaired with moderate ageing.
source: We show that behavioural and vascular responses to skin local environmental cooling are impaired with even moderate ageing, with reduced TRPM8 gene/protein expression especially.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Vascular responses to skin local environmental cooling are impaired with moderate ageing.
source: We show that behavioural and vascular responses to skin local environmental cooling are impaired with even moderate ageing, with reduced TRPM8 gene/protein expression especially.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: TRPM8 gene expression is reduced in ageing.
source: We show that behavioural and vascular responses to skin local environmental cooling are impaired with even moderate ageing, with reduced TRPM8 gene/protein expression especially.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by RT-PCR data in Figure 4h.

claim: TRPM8 protein expression is reduced in ageing.
source: We show that behavioural and vascular responses to skin local environmental cooling are impaired with even moderate ageing, with reduced TRPM8 gene/protein expression especially.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by western blot data in Figure 4i.

claim: Pharmacological blockade of TRPA1/TRPM8 substantially diminishes the cold-induced vascular response in aged mice compared with young mice.
source: Pharmacological blockade of the residual TRPA1/TRPM8 component substantially diminished the response in aged, compared with young mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: The cold-induced vascular response in ageing mice relies on remaining TRP receptor activity.
source: This implies the reliance of the already reduced cold-induced vascular response in ageing mice on remaining TRP receptor activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the pharmacological blockade experiments presented in the abstract.

claim: Sympathetic-induced vasoconstriction is reduced in ageing.
source: Moreover, sympathetic-induced vasoconstriction was reduced with downregulation of the α2c adrenoceptor expression in ageing.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: α2c adrenoceptor expression is downregulated in ageing.
source: Moreover, sympathetic-induced vasoconstriction was reduced with downregulation of the α2c adrenoceptor expression in ageing.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by western blot data in Figure 6e.

claim: The cold-induced vascular response is important for sensing cold and retaining body heat and health.
source: The cold-induced vascular response is important for sensing cold and retaining body heat and health.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Cold sensors essential for the neurovascular pathway decline as ageing onsets.
source: These findings reveal that cold sensors, essential for this neurovascular pathway, decline as ageing onsets.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: Cold exposure produces counterbalancing responses including shivering thermogenesis involving skeletal muscle.
source: Upon exposure to cold, depending on the type and intensity, several counterbalancing responses are produced, such as shivering thermogenesis involving skeletal muscle, or non-shivering thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue (BAT) and peripheral vasoconstriction in skin (Señarís et al., 2018, Morrison, Shaun F., Morrison and Nakamura, 2011; Morrison and Nakamura, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cold exposure produces counterbalancing responses including non-shivering thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue.
source: Upon exposure to cold, depending on the type and intensity, several counterbalancing responses are produced, such as shivering thermogenesis involving skeletal muscle, or non-shivering thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue (BAT) and peripheral vasoconstriction in skin (Señarís et al., 2018, Morrison, Shaun F., Morrison and Nakamura, 2011; Morrison and Nakamura, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cold exposure produces counterbalancing responses including peripheral vasoconstriction in skin.
source: Upon exposure to cold, depending on the type and intensity, several counterbalancing responses are produced, such as shivering thermogenesis involving skeletal muscle, or non-shivering thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue (BAT) and peripheral vasoconstriction in skin (Señarís et al., 2018, Morrison, Shaun F., Morrison and Nakamura, 2011; Morrison and Nakamura, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Thermo-sensors in the form of temperature-sensitive sensory receptors are distributed throughout the skin.
source: To produce such responses, thermo-sensors in the form of temperature-sensitive sensory receptors are distributed throughout the skin and are considered to work as a first line of defence against cold, which makes peripheral cutaneous responses a fundamental event in the defence against environmental thermal challenge.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Peripheral cutaneous responses are a fundamental event in the defence against environmental thermal challenge.
source: To produce such responses, thermo-sensors in the form of temperature-sensitive sensory receptors are distributed throughout the skin and are considered to work as a first line of defence against cold, which makes peripheral cutaneous responses a fundamental event in the defence against environmental thermal challenge.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Sensory receptors in the skin initiate the vascular cold constrictor response which acts to protect against body heat loss and prevent hypothermia.
source: The sensory receptors in the skin initiate the vascular cold constrictor response which acts to protect against body heat loss and prevent hypothermia.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The vascular cold constrictor response is followed by subsequent vasodilation, a restorative response essential to protect the affected skin against cold-induced conditions.
source: This response is followed by the subsequent vasodilation, a restorative response that is essential to protect the affected skin against cold-induced conditions, such as chilblains, trench foot, frostbite, and Raynaud's condition (Daanen and van der Struijs, 2005; Keatinge, 1957; Lewis, 1930).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cold-induced conditions include chilblains, trench foot, frostbite, and Raynaud's condition.
source: This response is followed by the subsequent vasodilation, a restorative response that is essential to protect the affected skin against cold-induced conditions, such as chilblains, trench foot, frostbite, and Raynaud's condition (Daanen and van der Struijs, 2005; Keatinge, 1957; Lewis, 1930).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The cold response is a finely tuned well-balanced response that maintains cellular function and physiological homeostasis during cold exposure.
source: It is a finely tuned well-balanced response that maintains cellular function and physiological homeostasis during cold exposure.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Physiological changes in ageing lead to dysfunctional signalling which causes a reduced adaptation to cold exposure.
source: Whilst this response is relevant to all ages, physiological changes in ageing leads to dysfunctional signalling which causes a reduced adaptation to cold exposure (Guergova and Dufour, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Lack of physical activity in the elderly population exacerbates the fall in core body temperature which can cause fatal cardiovascular and respiratory problems.
source: With the lack of physical activity in the elderly population, it exacerbates the fall in core body temperature which can cause fatal cardiovascular and respiratory problems (Billeter et al., 2014; Stares and Kosatsky, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In 2018, approximately 11,000 deaths linked to cold exposure occurred in England.
source: This is normally the biggest cause behind the National Health Service (NHS) excess winter deaths that we witness every year, where in 2018 it caused approximately 11,000 deaths linked to cold exposure in England (Office for National Statistics, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to official statistics.

claim: The cold-induced vascular response in mouse paw consists of a TRPA1/TRPM8-initiated sympathetic α2c adrenoceptor mediated neuronal vasoconstriction.
source: We have previously delineated the primary roles of transient receptor potential (TRP) channels in producing a distinctive biphasic vascular response to cold in the mouse paw consisting of a TRP ankyrin 1 (TRPA1)/ melastatin 8 (TRPM8)-initiated sympathetic α2c adrenoceptor mediated neuronal vasoconstriction and a distinct TRPA1-CGRP (Calcitonin gene-related peptide) mediated sensory-vasodilator component (Aubdool et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The cold-induced vascular response in mouse paw includes a distinct TRPA1-CGRP mediated sensory-vasodilator component.
source: We have previously delineated the primary roles of transient receptor potential (TRP) channels in producing a distinctive biphasic vascular response to cold in the mouse paw consisting of a TRP ankyrin 1 (TRPA1)/ melastatin 8 (TRPM8)-initiated sympathetic α2c adrenoceptor mediated neuronal vasoconstriction and a distinct TRPA1-CGRP (Calcitonin gene-related peptide) mediated sensory-vasodilator component (Aubdool et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: TRPA1 is a biomolecular sensor for reduced temperatures especially noxious cold (<18°C).
source: TRPA1 is a biomolecular sensor for reduced temperatures especially noxious cold ( < 18 °C), mediating aversive behaviour such as avoiding cold-induced pain, whilst also being involved in mediating inflammatory pain (Kwan et al., 2006; Nassini et al., 2014; Jain et al., 2011; Gouin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TRPA1 mediates aversive behaviour such as avoiding cold-induced pain.
source: TRPA1 is a biomolecular sensor for reduced temperatures especially noxious cold ( < 18 °C), mediating aversive behaviour such as avoiding cold-induced pain, whilst also being involved in mediating inflammatory pain (Kwan et al., 2006; Nassini et al., 2014; Jain et al., 2011; Gouin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TRPA1 is involved in mediating inflammatory pain.
source: TRPA1 is a biomolecular sensor for reduced temperatures especially noxious cold ( < 18 °C), mediating aversive behaviour such as avoiding cold-induced pain, whilst also being involved in mediating inflammatory pain (Kwan et al., 2006; Nassini et al., 2014; Jain et al., 2011; Gouin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TRPA1 activates C and Aδ sensory nerves to release neuropeptides such as CGRP to mediate neurogenic vasodilation.
source: Additionally, it activates C and Aδ sensory nerves to release neuropeptides such as CGRP to mediate neurogenic vasodilation (Aubdool et al., 2016; Story et al., 2003; Gentry et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TRPM8 is sensitive to low or reduced temperatures such as cool temperatures (<28°C).
source: TRPM8 on the other hand is sensitive to low or reduced temperatures such as cool temperatures ( < 28 °C) (McKemy et al., 2002; Peier et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TRPM8 is involved in deep body cooling.
source: It is involved in deep body cooling and suggested to supersede the role of TRPA1 (Gavva et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: TRPM8 is suggested to supersede the role of TRPA1 in deep body cooling.
source: It is involved in deep body cooling and suggested to supersede the role of TRPA1 (Gavva et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: TRPM8 is suggested to be a vasoactive stimulus.
source: TRPM8 is also suggested to be a vasoactive stimulus (Bautista et al., 2007; Johnson et al., 2005; Silva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The sympathetic α2c adrenoceptor mediates the vasoconstriction of the blood vessels.
source: The other established receptor that plays a pivotal role in cold signalling is the sympathetic α2c adrenoceptor, which mediates the vasoconstriction of the blood vessels (Bailey et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The sympathetic branch involved in the vasoconstrictor component of the cold response has reduced activity in ageing humans.
source: Whilst the sympathetic branch that is involved in the vasoconstrictor component of the cold response has been shown to have reduced activity in ageing humans (Holowatz et al., 2010; Degroot and Kenney, 2007), little is known about the functionality of the cold receptors TRPA1 and TRPM8 in ageing.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Little is known about the functionality of the cold receptors TRPA1 and TRPM8 in ageing.
source: Whilst the sympathetic branch that is involved in the vasoconstrictor component of the cold response has been shown to have reduced activity in ageing humans (Holowatz et al., 2010; Degroot and Kenney, 2007), little is known about the functionality of the cold receptors TRPA1 and TRPM8 in ageing.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: In young mice, cold treatment at 4°C produced a maximum vasoconstriction of 51.1% ± 1.1%.
source: In young mice, the cold treatment produced a maximum vasoconstriction of 51.1% ± 1.1%, however, in aged mice this was significantly blunted with maximum vasoconstriction of 27.7% ± 3.0% (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: In aged mice, cold treatment at 4°C produced a maximum vasoconstriction of 27.7% ± 3.0%.
source: In young mice, the cold treatment produced a maximum vasoconstriction of 51.1% ± 1.1%, however, in aged mice this was significantly blunted with maximum vasoconstriction of 27.7% ± 3.0% (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The maximum vasoconstriction in response to cold treatment is significantly blunted in aged mice compared to young mice.
source: In young mice, the cold treatment produced a maximum vasoconstriction of 51.1% ± 1.1%, however, in aged mice this was significantly blunted with maximum vasoconstriction of 27.7% ± 3.0% (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The area under the response curve (AUC) analysis showed a significantly greater vasoconstrictor response in young than aged mice.
source: These changes were reflected in the area under the response curve (AUC) analysis with a significantly greater response in young than aged mice (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The initial rate of blood flow recovery after cold treatment was significantly faster in young mice compared to aged mice.
source: Although blood flow did not fully recover back to the baseline, the initial rate of recovery immediately after maximum vasoconstriction before it slowly plateaued off was significantly faster in the young mice compared to the aged mice (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Blood flow did not fully recover back to baseline after cold treatment.
source: Although blood flow did not fully recover back to the baseline, the initial rate of recovery immediately after maximum vasoconstriction before it slowly plateaued off was significantly faster in the young mice compared to the aged mice (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The cold induced vascular response starts to diminish with ageing, affecting both parts of the vascular response.
source: These results suggest that with ageing the cold induced vascular response starts to diminish, which affects both parts of the vascular response.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Moderately aged mice (13-15 months) are equivalent to middle aged in human terms.
source: We were surprized that these changes were observed with moderately aged mice, equivalent to middle aged in human terms (Dutta and Sengupta, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: At 13-15 months of age, there is clear evidence of elevated gene expression in dorsal root ganglion (DRG) and skin of senescence markers P16 and P21.
source: However, at this age there is a clear evidence of elevated gene expression in dorsal root ganglion (DRG) and skin of senescence markers associated with ageing, P16; INK4A, cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 2 A (P16) and P21; Waf1, cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 1 (P21), (Figure 1g–h) also confirmed by western blotting (Figure 1i).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figures 1g-i.

claim: In young mice, cold treatment at 4°C produced a maximum vasoconstriction of 45.5% ± 3.0% as measured by laser Doppler imager.
source: In young mice, the cold treatment produced a maximum vasoconstriction of 45.5% ± 3.0%; however, in aged mice, this was significantly lower with a maximum vasoconstriction of 23.4% ± 4.7%, a result which was reflected in the AUC analysis (Figure 2b–c).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2b-c.

claim: In aged mice, cold treatment at 4°C produced a maximum vasoconstriction of 23.4% ± 4.7% as measured by laser Doppler imager.
source: In young mice, the cold treatment produced a maximum vasoconstriction of 45.5% ± 3.0%; however, in aged mice, this was significantly lower with a maximum vasoconstriction of 23.4% ± 4.7%, a result which was reflected in the AUC analysis (Figure 2b–c).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2b-c.

claim: Aged mice had a significantly higher baseline skin temperature than young mice.
source: There was a trend of greater reduction in skin temperature of aged mice after the cold-water treatment; however, the aged mice had a significantly higher skin temperature at baseline.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Aged mice are losing more body heat than young mice.
source: This suggests that they were losing more body heat and is consistent with the fact that the ability to maintain core body temperature declines with ageing (Figure 2d–f).
evidence: This is an inference from the baseline skin temperature data.

claim: The ability to maintain core body temperature declines with ageing.
source: This suggests that they were losing more body heat and is consistent with the fact that the ability to maintain core body temperature declines with ageing (Figure 2d–f).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Tissue oxygen saturation underwent a similar reduction in both young and aged mice after cold exposure.
source: The tissue oxygen saturation level underwent a similar reduction in both young and aged mice after the cold exposure (Figure 2g–h) but recovered more robustly in the young mice compared to the aged mice as shown by AUC analysis (Figure 2i).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2g-h.

claim: Tissue oxygen saturation recovered more robustly in young mice compared to aged mice after cold exposure.
source: The tissue oxygen saturation level underwent a similar reduction in both young and aged mice after the cold exposure (Figure 2g–h) but recovered more robustly in the young mice compared to the aged mice as shown by AUC analysis (Figure 2i).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2i.

claim: Protein expression of 3-nitrotyrosine (3-NT), a biomarker of oxidative stress, is elevated in aged hindpaw skin.
source: We also found evidence of increased cellular stress as protein expression of 3-nitrotyrosine (3-NT), a biomarker of oxidative stress produced via reactive nitrogen species was elevated in aged hindpaw skin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), in keeping with physiological ageing.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Aged mice showed a significant delayed latency for paw licking/paw withdrawal/jumping at 4°C compared to young mice.
source: At all three low/reduced temperatures, the aged mice showed a significant delayed latency for paw licking/paw withdrawal/jumping compared to the young mice, suggesting impaired cold sensing in aged mice (Figure 3a–c), but with little difference in the total number of responses observed among groups (Figure 3d-f).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Aged mice showed a significant delayed latency for paw licking/paw withdrawal/jumping at 10°C compared to young mice.
source: At all three low/reduced temperatures, the aged mice showed a significant delayed latency for paw licking/paw withdrawal/jumping compared to the young mice, suggesting impaired cold sensing in aged mice (Figure 3a–c), but with little difference in the total number of responses observed among groups (Figure 3d-f).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Aged mice showed a significant delayed latency for paw licking/paw withdrawal/jumping at 20°C compared to young mice.
source: At all three low/reduced temperatures, the aged mice showed a significant delayed latency for paw licking/paw withdrawal/jumping compared to the young mice, suggesting impaired cold sensing in aged mice (Figure 3a–c), but with little difference in the total number of responses observed among groups (Figure 3d-f).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: There is a reduction in sensitivity to cold with ageing at temperatures at which the cold sensors TRPA1 and TRPM8 are active.
source: These results indicate that there is a reduction in sensitivity to cold with ageing at temperatures at which the cold sensors TRPA1 and TRPM8 are active; thus leading us to hypothesise that at least one cold-sensitive TRP pathways deteriorates with ageing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cold plate behavioral data.

claim: The largest difference in response time compared with temperature between young and aged mice was observed at 20°C.
source: Here, the response time was compared with the overall temperatures tested. The largest difference in response time compared with temperature between young and aged mice was observed at 20 °C, in keeping with the TRPM8 activation range (Figure 3i).
evidence: This is a secondary analysis of the cold plate data shown in Figure 3i.

claim: The combined pre-treatment of A967079 and AMTB partially but significantly inhibited the vasoconstriction in young mice.
source: The combined pre-treatment of A967079 and AMTB partially but significantly inhibited the vasoconstriction in young mice.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 4a and d.

claim: The combined pre-treatment of A967079 and AMTB produced a more substantial inhibition of vascular responses induced by cold in aged mice compared to young mice.
source: By comparison, this treatment regime produced a more substantial inhibition of vascular responses induced by cold in the aged mice (Figure 4a and d).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 4a and d.

claim: The role of TRP receptors in the cold-induced vascular response remains as ageing occurs.
source: This result reveals that the role of TRP receptors in the cold-induced vascular response remains and suggests as ageing occurs the TRP-mediated signalling may become more important.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the antagonist treatment data.

claim: As ageing occurs, TRP-mediated signalling may become more important in the cold-induced vascular response.
source: This result reveals that the role of TRP receptors in the cold-induced vascular response remains and suggests as ageing occurs the TRP-mediated signalling may become more important.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the antagonist treatment data.

claim: A967079 treatment produced a similar effect to the combined antagonist treatment of A967079+AMTB, where the antagonist was more effective in aged than in young mice.
source: The A967079 treatment produced a similar effect to the combined antagonist treatment of A967079+ AMTB, where the antagonist was more effective in aged than in the young mice (Figure 4b and e).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 4b and e.

claim: AMTB treatment inhibited the cold-induced vascular response in young mice.
source: By comparison, the AMTB treatment inhibited the response in young mice, but had no significant effect in the vascular response to cold (Figure 4c and f) in aged mice.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 4c and f.

claim: AMTB treatment had no significant effect on the cold-induced vascular response in aged mice.
source: By comparison, the AMTB treatment inhibited the response in young mice, but had no significant effect in the vascular response to cold (Figure 4c and f) in aged mice.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 4c and f.

claim: As ageing occurs, TRPM8 loses its ability to respond to local cold treatment.
source: This provides further evidence that as ageing occurs, TRPM8 loses its ability to respond to local cold treatment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the AMTB treatment data.

claim: The level of Trpa1 mRNA in DRG is similar in both young and aged mice.
source: RT-PCR analysis of DRG showed similar level of Trpa1 mRNA in both young and aged mice (Figure 4g).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: The level of Trpm8 mRNA in DRG is significantly reduced in aged compared to young mice.
source: However, the level of Trpm8 mRNA was significantly reduced in the aged compared to the young mice (Figure 4h), as was its protein expression when analysed by western blot (Figure 4i).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 4h.

claim: TRPM8 protein expression in DRG is significantly reduced in aged compared to young mice.
source: However, the level of Trpm8 mRNA was significantly reduced in the aged compared to the young mice (Figure 4h), as was its protein expression when analysed by western blot (Figure 4i).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 4i.

claim: Topical application of menthol (10%) to the ear caused increased blood flow in young mice, which was significantly lower in aged mice.
source: The topical application of menthol (10%) to the ear caused increased blood flow in young mice, which was significantly lower in the aged mice (Figure 5a), as shown by the maximum increase in blood flow (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 5a-b.

claim: The AUC analysis of blood flow showed a significant increase with menthol treatment compared to vehicle in young mice, but not in aged mice.
source: The AUC analysis of blood flow showed a significant increase with menthol treatment compared to vehicle in young mice, but not in aged mice (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Topical application of cinnamaldehyde (10%) increased blood flow in young mice, which was significantly lower in aged mice.
source: Similarly, CA (10%) application also increased blood flow in young mice, however, this increase was significantly lower in aged mice (Figure 5d–e, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 5d-e.

claim: The AUC analysis showed a significant increase in blood flow with cinnamaldehyde treatment compared to vehicle in young mice but not in aged mice.
source: The AUC analysis showed a significant increase in blood flow with CA treatment compared to vehicle in young mice but not in aged mice (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: TRPA1 and TRPM8-mediated vasoactive activity starts to deteriorate in moderate ageing.
source: These findings suggest that the TRPA1 and TRPM8-mediated vasoactive activity starts to deteriorate in moderate ageing, and it is not exclusive to cold signalling.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the menthol and cinnamaldehyde treatment data.

claim: Topical application of 10% capsaicin produced a similar increase in ear blood flow in both young and aged mice.
source: The topical application of 10 % capsaicin produced a similar increase in ear blood flow in both young and aged mice (Figure 5g–i) indicating, unlike TRPA1 and TRPM8 signalling, TRPV1 signalling does not deteriorate with ageing.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 5g-i.

claim: Unlike TRPA1 and TRPM8 signalling, TRPV1 signalling does not deteriorate with ageing.
source: The topical application of 10 % capsaicin produced a similar increase in ear blood flow in both young and aged mice (Figure 5g–i) indicating, unlike TRPA1 and TRPM8 signalling, TRPV1 signalling does not deteriorate with ageing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the capsaicin treatment data.

claim: Intraplantar injection of noradrenaline revealed a significantly greater reduction of blood flow in young mice compared to aged mice.
source: The response to the intraplantar injection of the non-selective and endogenous sympathetic neurotransmitter noradrenaline (NA) revealed a significantly greater reduction of blood flow in young mice compared to aged mice (Figure 6a–b).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 6a-b.

claim: Medetomidine caused immediate vasoconstriction that was blunted in aged mice compared to young mice.
source: Medetomidine caused immediate vasoconstriction as expected, but the response was blunted in aged mice compared to young mice (Figure 6c–d).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 6c-d.

claim: Western blotting analysis of the hind paw skin showed a significant reduction in the expression of α2c adrenoceptor in aged mice.
source: The western blotting analysis of the hind paw skin showed a significant reduction in the expression of α2c adrenoceptor in aged mice (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: Tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) showed a similar level of expression in both young and aged mice.
source: Tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), an enzyme that catalyses the rate limiting stage of noradrenaline synthesis, showed a similar level of expression (Figure 6f) including of its active form, phosphorylated TH in both young and aged mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting the production of noradrenaline remained unaltered with ageing.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 6f.

claim: Phosphorylated TH showed a similar level of expression in both young and aged mice.
source: Tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), an enzyme that catalyses the rate limiting stage of noradrenaline synthesis, showed a similar level of expression (Figure 6f) including of its active form, phosphorylated TH in both young and aged mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting the production of noradrenaline remained unaltered with ageing.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The production of noradrenaline remained unaltered with ageing.
source: Tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), an enzyme that catalyses the rate limiting stage of noradrenaline synthesis, showed a similar level of expression (Figure 6f) including of its active form, phosphorylated TH in both young and aged mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting the production of noradrenaline remained unaltered with ageing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the TH expression data.

claim: In ageing, the expression and function of the α2c adrenoceptor diminishes and contributes to the impaired constrictor response against cold.
source: This indicates that in ageing the expression and function of the α2c adrenoceptor diminishes and that contributes to the impaired constrictor response against cold.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the α2c adrenoceptor expression and function data.

claim: α2a adrenoceptor gene expression in DRG is reduced in ageing.
source: To elucidate this, we first investigated DRG and found that α2a and α2cc adrenoceptor gene expression was reduced in ageing (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a-b) similar to that shown for the Trpm8 gene, (Figure 4h) whilst no significant difference was found for Trpv1 receptors (Figure 7—figure supplement 1c) in keeping with results for Trpa1 (Figure 4g).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1a.

claim: α2c adrenoceptor gene expression in DRG is reduced in ageing.
source: To elucidate this, we first investigated DRG and found that α2a and α2cc adrenoceptor gene expression was reduced in ageing (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a-b) similar to that shown for the Trpm8 gene, (Figure 4h) whilst no significant difference was found for Trpv1 receptors (Figure 7—figure supplement 1c) in keeping with results for Trpa1 (Figure 4g).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1b.

claim: No significant difference was found for Trpv1 receptor gene expression in DRG between young and aged mice.
source: To elucidate this, we first investigated DRG and found that α2a and α2cc adrenoceptor gene expression was reduced in ageing (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a-b) similar to that shown for the Trpm8 gene, (Figure 4h) whilst no significant difference was found for Trpv1 receptors (Figure 7—figure supplement 1c) in keeping with results for Trpa1 (Figure 4g).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The gene expression of both Trpa1 and Trpm8 in sympathetic ganglia (SG) were significantly downregulated in aged mice.
source: The RT-PCR data on SG showed the gene expression of both Trpa1 and Trpm8 in young and aged mice. Interestingly, the expression of both receptors were significantly downregulated in aged mice (Figure 7a–b).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 7a-b.

claim: Western blot analysis of TRPM8 on SG showed diminished expression in aged mice compared to young mice.
source: Whilst there is no feasible selective TRPA1 antibody available, western blot analysis of TRPM8 on SG recapitulated the qPCR finding of diminished expression in aged mice compared to young mice (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: Cold TRP receptors are expressed in sympathetic neurons and are diminished in ageing.
source: These findings reveal expression of cold TRP receptors in sympathetic neurons which are diminished in ageing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the gene and protein expression data from sympathetic ganglia.

claim: The TRPM8 agonist menthol (300 µM) caused an increase in calcium in cultured sympathetic ganglia cells.
source: The TRPM8 agonist menthol (300 µM) caused an increase in calcium as measured by the change in fura-2 fluorescence ratio compared to vehicle (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: The calcium response to menthol in cultured sympathetic ganglia cells was significantly reduced in the presence of the TRPM8 antagonist AMTB (10 µM).
source: This response was significantly reduced in the presence of the TRPM8 antagonist AMTB (10 µM) (Figure 7d–e).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 7d-e.

claim: The TRPA1 agonist AITC (200 µM) caused an increase in calcium in cultured sympathetic ganglia cells.
source: Similarly, the TRPA1 agonist Allyl isothiocyanate (AITC) (200 µM) also caused an increase in calcium in these cultured cells compared to vehicle (Figure 7f), which was significantly inhibited by the TRPA1 antagonist A967079 (10 µM) (Figure 7f–g).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 7f.

claim: The calcium response to AITC in cultured sympathetic ganglia cells was significantly inhibited by the TRPA1 antagonist A967079 (10 µM).
source: Similarly, the TRPA1 agonist Allyl isothiocyanate (AITC) (200 µM) also caused an increase in calcium in these cultured cells compared to vehicle (Figure 7f), which was significantly inhibited by the TRPA1 antagonist A967079 (10 µM) (Figure 7f–g).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 7f-g.

claim: TRPM8 and TRPA1 receptors are expressed in sympathetic neurons and activate sympathetic nerves.
source: These results show that TRPM8 and TRPA1 receptors are expressed in sympathetic neurons and activate sympathetic nerves.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the calcium imaging data from cultured sympathetic ganglia cells.

claim: Cold stimuli activate TRPA1 and TRPM8 channels on sympathetic nerves, which induces calcium-dependent release of vesicles containing NA into the synaptic cleft where they activate the α2c adrenoceptor on smooth muscle cells to mediate vasoconstriction.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that cold stimuli activate TRPA1 and TRPM8 channels on sympathetic nerves, which induces calcium-dependent release of vesicles containing NA into the synaptic cleft where they activate the α2c adrenoceptor on smooth muscle cells to mediate vasoconstriction (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the collective findings of the study.

claim: This signalling cascade has been shown in PC12 cells, an in vitro model for sympathetic neurons.
source: This signalling cascade has been shown in PC12 cells, an in vitro model for sympathetic neurons (Smith et al., 2004; Peixoto-Neves et al., 2018; Yoshimura et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There is a potential for sympathetic-sensory interactive signalling in skin, which weakens as ageing progresses.
source: It indicates a potential for sympathetic-sensory interactive signalling in skin, which weakens as ageing progresses, in turn affecting the sensitivity of the vascular response to cold.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the collective findings.

claim: The role of TRPA1 and TRPM8 as cold-sensitive thermoreceptors is established.
source: The role of TRPA1 and TRPM8 as cold-sensitive thermoreceptors is established (Story et al., 2003; Bautista et al., 2007; Karashima et al., 2009; Peier et al., 2002; McKemy et al., 2002) and our research has demonstrated the essential role they play as vascular cold sensors (Aubdool et al., 2014; Pan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TRPA1 and TRPM8 play an essential role as vascular cold sensors.
source: The role of TRPA1 and TRPM8 as cold-sensitive thermoreceptors is established (Story et al., 2003; Bautista et al., 2007; Karashima et al., 2009; Peier et al., 2002; McKemy et al., 2002) and our research has demonstrated the essential role they play as vascular cold sensors (Aubdool et al., 2014; Pan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: The expression and activity of TRPM8 is significantly diminished in ageing.
source: We provide a new insight into the changing roles of TRPA1 and TRPM8 in the vascular response to cold in ageing; the expression and activity of TRPM8 is significantly diminished, and to a lesser extent TRPA1-mediated signalling too.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: TRPA1-mediated signalling is diminished to a lesser extent than TRPM8 in ageing.
source: We provide a new insight into the changing roles of TRPA1 and TRPM8 in the vascular response to cold in ageing; the expression and activity of TRPM8 is significantly diminished, and to a lesser extent TRPA1-mediated signalling too.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The vascular response to cold is functionally deficient in ageing.
source: The vascular response to the cold is a primary physiological response, which we have previously teased out the key mechanisms for, consisting of TRPA1/M8 initiated α2c-mediated sympathetic vasoconstriction followed by TRPA1/M8-mediated sensory vascular relaxation after localised cold exposure in the mouse paw. Here, we show that the response is functionally deficient in ageing as measured by two different laser blood flow measurement techniques.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings using FLPI and laser Doppler techniques.

claim: Both components of the cold-induced vascular response were impaired in ageing with blunted vasoconstriction that will lead to increased heat loss.
source: Both components of the cold-induced vascular response were impaired in ageing with blunted vasoconstriction that will lead to increased heat loss, and a slower rate of recovery that may lead to cold-induced injuries (Keatinge, 1957; Roustit et al., 2011; Herrick, 2005).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings with speculation about consequences.

claim: A slower rate of recovery in the cold-induced vascular response may lead to cold-induced injuries.
source: Both components of the cold-induced vascular response were impaired in ageing with blunted vasoconstriction that will lead to increased heat loss, and a slower rate of recovery that may lead to cold-induced injuries (Keatinge, 1957; Roustit et al., 2011; Herrick, 2005).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental findings and supported by citations.

claim: Ageing-induced pathological conditions and frailty appear at a later age, but the underlying physiological changes begin at middle age of around 40 years old in humans.
source: This finding is in keeping with the concept that although ageing-induced pathological conditions and frailty appear at a later age, the underlying physiological changes that manifest those conditions begin at a middle age of around 40 years old in humans.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Brain volume and weight start to reduce at around 40 years old in humans.
source: Indeed, this is when the brain volume and weight start to reduce Peters, 2006; cardiovascular functions begin to decline and elite athletes start to lose stamina (Pal et al., 2014; Mühlberg and Platt, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Cardiovascular functions begin to decline at around 40 years old in humans.
source: Indeed, this is when the brain volume and weight start to reduce Peters, 2006; cardiovascular functions begin to decline and elite athletes start to lose stamina (Pal et al., 2014; Mühlberg and Platt, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Elite athletes start to lose stamina at around 40 years old.
source: Indeed, this is when the brain volume and weight start to reduce Peters, 2006; cardiovascular functions begin to decline and elite athletes start to lose stamina (Pal et al., 2014; Mühlberg and Platt, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The finding of diminished TRPM8 expression with ageing is indicative of a major influence of this channel that would lead to the impaired response to cold observed in ageing.
source: We consider that the finding of diminished TRPM8 expression with ageing is indicative of a major influence of this channel that would lead to the impaired response to cold observed in ageing, such as in the cold induced vascular response.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.
